intro.html: Some people notice when others are hurting and do something about it. Others notice and shrug, or even make things worse. English has a rich set of words for both kinds of heart, and good writers choose among them carefully: a considerate neighbor and a magnanimous rival are kind in different ways, and a callous boss is cruel in a different way from a vindictive one.

Warm hearts: compassionate (feels for others’ pain), considerate (thinks of others), altruistic (helps with no reward), humane (merciful), magnanimous (generous to a rival), solicitous (anxiously caring). Cold hearts: callous (unfeeling), ruthless (pitiless), vindictive (wants revenge), spiteful (mean out of petty ill will).

words.def: feeling for others who suffer and wanting to help them
words.ex: The {compassionate} nurse held the frightened boy’s hand until his parents arrived.
words.ctx: Instead of laughing when the runner tripped, the {compassionate} crowd went silent, and two of her rivals stopped to help her to her feet.
words.etym: From Latin compati, “to suffer with”: com (with) + pati (to suffer).

mn.text: Maya’s heart works like a compass: it always points her toward whoever is hurting. She is {compassionate}.

scene.alt: A teenage girl kneels beside a crying boy on the playground and offers him a bandage.

words.def: careful not to hurt, bother or inconvenience others
words.ex: It was {considerate} of Omar to call ahead and say he would be late.
words.ctx: The upstairs neighbors were unusually {considerate}: knowing the baby napped at noon, they always waited until two o’clock to vacuum.

mn.text: Before Jonah bangs his drum, he stops to consider it: is the baby asleep? Thinking of others first makes him {considerate}.

scene.alt: A teenage boy sets down his drum and shushes because his baby brother is napping.

words.def: helping others with no thought of reward for oneself
words.ex: The {altruistic} teen spent her summer teaching little kids to swim for free.
words.ctx: Her reasons for volunteering were purely {altruistic}: she asked for no pay, no thanks and no mention of her name in the newsletter.
words.etym: From French altruisme, built on Italian altrui, “of others,” from Latin alter, “other.”

mn.text: Al shovels every neighbor’s walk and waves away their money. Al truly helps for nothing in return: he is {altruistic}.

scene.alt: A man named Al, holding a snow shovel, waves away the coins an old woman offers him.

words.def: kind and merciful; causing no needless pain
words.ex: The shelter found a {humane} way to catch the stray cats without hurting them.
words.ctx: The old rules let farm animals be kept in cramped cages, but the new law is more {humane}: every animal must have room to move, fresh water and shelter.
words.etym: From Latin humanus, “human”; humane began as another spelling of human and came to mean kind and gentle.
words.note: Humane (hyoo-MAYN) means kind and merciful; human (HYOO-mun) means a person, or having to do with people.

mn.text: Add an E to human for Extra kindness: Ada’s {humane} trap catches the mouse without a scratch, and she lets it go in the garden.

scene.alt: A woman kneels in a garden and lets a mouse run free from a box trap.

words.def: generous and forgiving, especially toward a rival
words.ex: In a {magnanimous} gesture, the champion invited the runner-up to share the stage.
words.ctx: After winning the chess final, Ada was {magnanimous}: instead of gloating, she praised her opponent’s bold opening and offered to practice with him.
words.etym: From Latin magnanimus, “great-souled”: magnus (great) + animus (mind, soul).

mn.text: Dev wins the race, then lifts the trophy with the runner-up and cheers for him too. A heart that big toward a rival is {magnanimous}.

scene.alt: The winner of a race offers to share his trophy with the surprised runner-up.

words.def: eagerly caring about someone’s comfort and well-being
words.ex: The {solicitous} host kept asking whether everyone had enough to eat.
words.ctx: Grandpa had only a mild cold, but Lila was so {solicitous} that she brought him tea, tucked in his blanket and checked on him every ten minutes.

mn.text: “So, list us your needs: tea? a pillow? another blanket?” Lila fusses over Granny Mae’s sniffle. She is {solicitous}.

scene.alt: A girl offers tea to her grandmother on the sofa and asks what else she needs.

words.def: unfeeling toward other people’s pain or trouble
words.ex: Laughing at the boy who dropped his lunch tray was a {callous} thing to do.
words.ctx: The landlord’s answer to the flooded families was {callous}: he said their ruined furniture was not his problem and went back to his lunch.
words.etym: From Latin callosus, “hard-skinned,” from callum, hard skin.
words.note: Callous (unfeeling) sounds just like callus, the patch of hard skin a hand gets from hard work.

mn.text: A callus is hard skin that feels nothing. Rex walks past the crying girl without a glance, as if his heart had a callus: he is {callous}.

scene.alt: A man walks away without caring while a girl cries over her dropped ice cream.

words.def: showing no pity; willing to hurt others to get one’s way
words.ex: Lin is a {ruthless} checkers player who never lets anyone take back a move.
words.ctx: The new owner was {ruthless}: he closed the beloved bakery, let every worker go without warning and never once looked back.
words.etym: From the old word ruth, “pity,” + -less: without pity.

mn.text: Ruth is an old word for pity. The cartoon king who takes the farmers’ very last pears has no ruth at all: he is {ruthless}.

scene.alt: A cartoon king points and orders that a sad farmer’s last basket of fruit be taken.

words.def: wanting revenge; set on paying someone back
words.ex: After losing at checkers, my {vindictive} cousin hid the winner’s shoes.
words.ctx: Most fans forgave the referee’s honest mistake, but one {vindictive} fan spent the whole season writing letters demanding that he be fired.

mn.text: Vin keeps a whole dictionary of everyone who ever wronged him, and he plans to pay back every one. Vin is {vindictive}.

scene.alt: A man named Vin reads a book of grudges and plans his payback.

words.def: mean on purpose, out of petty ill will
words.ex: The {spiteful} cat stared right at me and pushed my cup off the table.
words.ctx: Jealous that her brother got the bigger room, she did something {spiteful}: she hid his favorite cap where he would not find it for weeks.
words.etym: From spite, a shortening of despite, which once meant scorn.

mn.text: Dinner was late, so Mittens looks Felix in the eye and slowly pushes his cup off the table: a {spiteful} cat.

scene.alt: A sneaky cat on a table pushes a cup off the edge while its owner gasps.

cold opposite
the difference
rows: feels another’s pain / feels nothing for it
forgives a rival / wants to pay a rival back
spares needless pain / shows no pity
careful not to bother others / bothers others on purpose
after.cap: Four kind words and the cruel words that mirror them.

after.html: Two sound-alike traps: humane (hyoo-MAYN, kind) is not human (a person), and callous (unfeeling) is not callus (a patch of hard skin). And magnanimous is about a big heart, never a big size.

items.q: The new trap catches mice without hurting them, so they can be let go outside. The trap is…
items.why: Humane (with an e) means kind and causing no needless pain. Human means a person.

items.q: True or false: magnanimous describes something very large in size.
items.why: False. magn- does mean great, but magnanimous is about a great heart: generous and forgiving, especially toward a rival.

choices: His callous joke about the lost puppy made Zoe cry.
Years of guitar playing left a callous on his thumb.
The callous blanket kept the baby warm.
items.why: Callous describes an unfeeling person or act. The hard patch of skin is spelled callus.

items.q: After losing the tennis final, Rosa shook the winner’s hand and praised her serve to the crowd. Rosa was being…
items.why: Being generous and gracious toward a rival is magnanimous. A vindictive player would want to pay the winner back.

choices: paying for a stranger’s groceries and slipping away before anyone can say thanks
lending a friend money so he will owe you a favor
helping a neighbor so he will praise you to everyone
items.why: An altruistic act helps others with no thought of reward: no favor owed, no praise wanted.
